strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: addresses the fundamental disconnect between parametric factual knowledge acquisition (via SFT) and procedural reasoning/execution skills (via RL) in continual LLM adaptation.

Insightful geometric analysis: provides empirical evidence and control experiments showing that SFT and RL weight updates occupy nearly orthogonal subspaces, supported by a formal theoretical derivation in the appendix demonstrating functional signal disentanglement under standard activation assumptions.

The proposed Parametric Skill Transfer (PaST) framework is simple, modular, and computationally efficient, bypassing costly on-policy RL rollouts on new target data via vector arithmetic and iterative skill bootstrapping.

Thorough empirical evaluation across diverse domains: benchmarks span closed-book short-context QA (SQuAD), massive long-context retrieval (LooGLE), and multi-turn closed-book tool-use execution across 20 unseen categories (StableToolBench), showing consistent and substantial gains over strong baselines like SEAL.

Insightful ablation experiments confirming the utility of iterative refinement over single-round scaling and demonstrating why post-hoc composition outperforms sequential fine-tuning and pre-injection.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a single model family (Qwen2.5-7B / Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct); evaluating on other distinct architectures (e.g., Llama 3) would strengthen the universality of the orthogonality and skill transfer claims.

Evaluation heavily relies on proprietary LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4.1) across SQuAD, LooGLE, and ToolBench, which can introduce evaluation noise or potential bias without reporting standard deterministic lexical/semantic metrics (e.g., exact match / token F1 on SQuAD).

The injection scaling factor lambda is fixed to 1 across all setups without an ablation or sensitivity analysis exploring how varying lambda influences the trade-off between knowledge retention and skill execution.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated premise addressing the critical gap between factual memorization via SFT and procedural reasoning/execution via RL in parametric continual adaptation.

Interesting and well-supported empirical finding demonstrating that parameter updates for declarative knowledge (SFT) and reasoning skills (RL) reside in nearly orthogonal subspaces, supported by a convincing control experiment (SFT vs. SFT) and theoretical analysis in activation space.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse domains and scales, including closed-book QA on standard contexts (SQuAD), long contexts (>21k tokens on LooGLE), and multi-turn agentic execution (ToolBench), demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines such as SEAL.

Thorough ablation studies verifying both the design choice of post-hoc composition over pre-injection/sequential fine-tuning and the necessity of iterative bootstrapping to decouple reasoning logic from source factual content.
Extensive implementation and experimental details provided in the appendix, including prompts, training configurations, and case studies, facilitating reproducibility.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a single model family and size (Qwen2.5-7B / Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), leaving open whether the observed parameter orthogonality and linear transferability generalize across different architectural styles (e.g., Llama, Mistral) or significantly larger parameter scales.

Evaluation heavily depends on proprietary LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4.1) for scoring SQuAD, LooGLE, and ToolBench outcomes, without reporting agreement rates with human evaluation or assessing judge calibration and variance.

The test sets for several ToolBench categories contain very few solvable evaluation queries (e.g., 3 to 5 queries for Advertising, SMS, AI & ML, Science), which makes category-level success rates noisy even though the aggregate trend across all 20 domains is positive.

The scaling factor $\lambda$ in the injection formula is fixed to 1.0 across all setups; a sensitivity analysis exploring the impact of varying $\lambda$ across different domains and tasks is missing.

strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: The paper addresses a fundamental limitation in continual knowledge updating, namely the disconnect between factual memorization (via SFT) and procedural reasoning/manipulation (via RL), and offers a lightweight solution that avoids expensive on-policy RL in new domains.

Insightful geometric analysis: The empirical demonstration of parameter orthogonality between SFT and RL updates, supported by a proper control experiment (comparing SFT-SFT vs. SFT-RL updates in Appendix B) and theoretical activation-space derivation (Appendix C), provides a sound motivation for task vector arithmetic.

Broad and consistent empirical validation: The framework is evaluated across three diverse regimes—closed-book QA (SQuAD), long-context retrieval over 21k+ token documents (LooGLE), and zero-shot multi-turn agentic tool use across 20 unseen categories (ToolBench)—demonstrating consistent and significant performance gains over strong baselines (e.g., SEAL).

Thorough ablation studies and practical training strategy: The iterative skill bootstrapping strategy and comparison of injection stages (post-hoc composition vs. sequential fine-tuning vs. pre-injection) convincingly justify the design choices of PaST.
High clarity and reproducibility: The paper and appendices provide extensive implementation details, prompts, reward formulations, training hyperparameter tables, and qualitative case studies.
weaknesses: Single model family evaluated: The empirical evaluation is conducted exclusively on Qwen2.5-7B models. Evaluating across another architecture or family (e.g., Llama-3) would substantiate the claim that SFT-RL update orthogonality and linear transferability are general phenomena.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-a-judge: Evaluation across SQuAD, LooGLE, and ToolBench solution rewards relies heavily on GPT-4.1 without reporting human validation, calibration, or error analysis of the judge's scoring consistency.

Omission of side-effect evaluation on general capabilities: The paper evaluates task-specific improvements on target domains but does not measure whether injecting the skill vector causes collateral degradation or forgetting on unrelated general benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K, or standard instruction-following).

Missing model merging baselines: While compared against standard SFT, sequential fine-tuning, and SEAL, the paper lacks comparisons against established weight-space composition methods (e.g., TIES-merging, DARE) or tuning the vector scaling coefficient lambda.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated empirical observation demonstrating that parameter updates for factual knowledge injection (via SFT) and procedural reasoning/skill acquisition (via RL) occupy nearly orthogonal subspaces.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse tasks, including closed-book question answering (SQuAD), long-context reasoning (LooGLE), and multi-turn agentic execution (ToolBench), demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines such as SEAL.

Well-designed control experiments and ablations, including verifying non-orthogonality between two SFT updates, sweeping iteration rounds vs. shard sizes in the iterative bootstrapping strategy, and comparing post-hoc injection against sequential fine-tuning and pre-injection.
Valuable efficiency analysis demonstrating that post-hoc linear injection matches the performance of extensive test-time target RL without incurring on-policy rollout overhead at test time.
weaknesses: All primary experiments and parameter update analyses are conducted exclusively on the Qwen2.5-7B family (Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct); empirical claims of orthogonality and transferability would be significantly strengthened by validating across other model families (e.g., Llama 3).

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4.1) across all evaluation benchmarks (SQuAD, LooGLE, and ToolBench trajectory judging) without validation against human judgments or calibration for potential judge biases.

The agentic tool-use environment relies on a synthetic simulator (GPT-4o-mini) rather than executing against live API environments, which may introduce simulation artifacts or lenient error tolerance into the reported success rates.

The linear composition coefficient lambda is fixed to 1.0 across all settings without an empirical sensitivity analysis exploring how varying vector scaling affects knowledge retention versus procedural execution.

strengths: Compelling conceptual framing that tackles a fundamental bottleneck in continual model adaptation: the functional disconnect between declarative knowledge acquisition (SFT) and procedural reasoning/execution capabilities (RL).

Solid empirical and theoretical backing: The paper demonstrates that parameter updates induced by SFT and RL are nearly orthogonal across layers and modules (supported by meaningful control experiments comparing SFT-to-SFT updates), and provides a formal derivation connecting parameter orthogonality to activation-space functional disentanglement.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation spanning three distinct evaluation scenarios: closed-book knowledge incorporation (SQuAD), long-context understanding (LooGLE), and zero-shot cross-domain agentic tool execution (ToolBench across 20 unseen categories).

Insightful ablation experiments that justify key architectural decisions, including the iterative bootstrapping strategy (analyzing the K x M trade-off), the transfer order (post-hoc composition vs. sequential fine-tuning vs. pre-injection), and cost-performance trade-offs against target-side RL.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a single model family and size (Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Validating whether parameter orthogonality and linear transferability hold across other model families (e.g., Llama 3) and differing parameter scales would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.

Heavily reliant on LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4.1 / GPT-4o-mini) for both the RL reward modeling and downstream benchmark scoring, without calibration against human evaluations or detailed error analysis regarding judge consistency.

The scaling parameter lambda is statically set to 1.0 across all experiments without sensitivity analysis or exploration of layer-wise weighting, leaving open the question of how sensitive target performance is to the magnitude of the injected skill vector.
